FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe the anatomy of the flexor tendons and the flexor sheath in the finger.
Determine options for repair and reconstruction of the flexor tendon.
Assess the complexity of flexor tendon injuries and their complications.
Overview
Zone II flexor tendon injuries frequently involve the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) and the
flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) tendons. Because of historically poor outcomes, this zone
was once termed no-man’s-land, and primary repair was not recommended. Improvements in

suture techniques and postoperative rehabilitation protocols have made it possible to achieve
a good result in zone II flexor tendon injuries, but they are still troublesome injuries.
The goals of surgical management are a repair construct that is strong enough for exercises
and, ideally, some active motion and effort to limit binding of the repair in the flexor sheath.
Recent suggestions include repair with the patient under local anesthesia to allow for
assessment of tendon repair site gliding through the pulleys and judicious venting (partial or
complete excision) of part of the A2 pulley and part or all of the A4 pulley to limit adhesions.
Epidemiology
Flexor tendon injuries are uncommon, with an incidence of 4.8 per 100,000 individuals per
year.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The FDS and FDP flex the digits, and the flexor pollicis longus (FPL) flexes the thumb.
The FDS arises from the medial epicondyle of the humerus, ulna, and radius and divides into
four bundles, separating into a superficial layer and a deep layer in the middle of the
forearm.
The superficial layer consists of the tendons to the long and ring fingers, and the deep layer
consists of the tendons to the index and little fingers.
The FDS tendons insert onto the shaft of the middle phalanx and act as the primary proximal
interphalangeal (PIP) joint flexor.
The long, ring, and little finger FDP tendons usually arise from a common muscle belly,
whereas the index finger FDP tendon typically arises separately and has greater
independence.
Tendons of the nine digital flexors enter the proximal carpal tunnel such that the four FDP
tendons are deep to the FDS tendons of the index and little fingers and the FDS tendons of
the ring and long digits lie superficial and ulnar or subadjacent to the median nerve. The FPL
lies deep and radial within the carpal tunnel adjacent to the scaphoid and trapezium.
As the FDS enters the A1 pulley, it divides into two slips through which the FDP tendon
passes.
The FDS to the little finger may be very narrow and occasionally is absent.
The two slips of the FDS rejoin deep to the FDP tendon over the distal aspect of the proximal
phalanx and the palmar plate of the PIP joint at the Camper chiasm and then insert as two

separate slips on the volar aspect of the middle phalanx.
Within zones I and II, the tendons are covered by visceral and parietal paratenon, and this
structure is the gliding surface.
The FDS and FDP tendons in the digits are surrounded by a pulley system composed of five
annular and three cruciate pulleys. The annular pulleys are thicker and stiffer, and the
cruciate pulleys are collapsible and flexible. The A1, A3, and A5 pulleys originate from the
palmar plates of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP), PIP, and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints.
The A2 and A4 pulleys originate from the middle halves of the proximal and middle
phalanges, respectively. The cruciate pulleys are located between A2 and A3 (C1 pulley),
between A3 and A4 (C2 pulley), and between A4 and A5 (C4 pulley; Figure 1).
In the index, long, ring, and little fingers, the A2 and A4 pulleys are the most important
pulleys biomechanically. The thumb contains two annular pulleys and one oblique pulley
between the two (order is from proximal to distal: A1 pulley, oblique pulley, A2 pulley). The
oblique pulley is the most important in prevention of bowstringing of the FPL.
Figure 1 Lateral (A) and dorsal (B) view illustrations of a finger show the components of the
digital flexor sheath. The sturdy annular pulleys (A1, A2, A3, A4, and A5) keep the tendons
closely applied to the phalanges. The thin, pliable cruciate pulleys (C1, C2, and C3) collapse to
allow digital flexion. The palmar aponeurosis (PA) pulley adds to the biomechanical efficiency
of the pulley system. (Reproduced from Strickland JW: Flexor tendon injuries: I. Foundations
of treatment. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 1995;3[1]:44-54.)

Vascular Anatomy
The blood supply of the flexor tendons is via the long and short vincular connections (Figure
2).
The FDP muscle belly blood supply in the forearm is predominantly from the ulnar artery.
The FPL muscle belly is supplied by the radial artery.
The FDS muscle belly is supplied by the radial and ulnar arteries.
Figure 2 Illustration of a finger shows the blood supply to the flexor tendons within the digital
sheath. The segmental vascular supply to the flexor tendons is via long and short vincular
connections. The vinculum brevis superficialis (VBS) and the vinculum brevis profundus (VBP)
consist of small triangular mesenteries near the insertion of the flexor digitorum superficialis
and flexor digitorum profundus tendons. The vinculum longum to the superficialis tendon
(VLS) arises from the floor of the digital sheath of the proximal phalanx. The vinculum longum
to the profundus tendon (VLP) arises from the superficialis at the level of the proximal
interphalangeal joint. The cutaway view shows the relative avascularity of the palmar side of
the flexor tendons in zones I and II compared with the richer blood supply on the dorsal side,
which connects with the vincula. (Reproduced with permission from Seiler JG III: Flexor tendon
injury, in Wolfe SW, Hotchkiss RN, Pederson WC, Kozin SH, Cohen MS, eds: Green's Operative
Hand Surgery, ed 7. Philadelphia, PA, Elsevier, 2017, vol 1, pp 183-230.)
Neural Anatomy

9/3/26, 4:20 PM
AAOS | Hand and Wrist Flexor Tendon Repair and Reconstruction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004034
4/29

The innervation of the FDS muscle is from the median nerve and enters the muscle belly in the
proximal forearm.
The FDP has dual innervation; the ring and little FDP are innervated by the ulnar nerve, and the
anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve innervates the index and long finger FDP.
The FPL is innervated by the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve.
Tendons
Tendon structure
Tendons are organized groups of fascicles containing longitudinally oriented bundles of
collagen (primarily type I) and fibroblasts called tenocytes.
Individual fascicles are covered by endotenon.
Epitenon covers groups of tendon fascicles.
Visceral paratenon and parietal paratenon line the surface of the tendon and the
undersurface of the tendon sheath, respectively.
Flexor tendon nutrition
Flexor tendons are perfused by a network of vessels, including longitudinal vessels entering
the tendon in the palm and extending down the intratendinous channels, segmental vessels
from the digital arteries that supply the tendon through the long and short vincula, and
vessels that enter the tendon at their respective insertions.
In the relatively avascular watershed areas, particularly over the proximal phalanx, tendon
nutrition is accomplished by synovial fluid diffusion via a process called imbibition.
Tendon healing
Phases of tendon healing
Inflammatory phase (time of injury to 7 days postinjury)—Fibroblast and macrophage
migration to the site of injury results in phagocytosis of the clot and necrotic tissue. During
this phase, repair strength relies entirely on the strength of the suture used.
Proliferative phase (1 to 3 weeks post injury)—Neovascularization begins. An increasing
number of fibroblasts deposit immature type III collagen, which is later replaced by type I
collagen. Tendon repairs do not accrue tensile strength until the beginning of the
remodeling phase.
Remodeling phase (3 to 12 weeks postinjury)—Collagen fibers become organized along the
length of the tendon.
Mechanisms of tendon healing

5/29

Extrinsic tendon healing involves inflammatory cells and fibroblasts derived from the
tendon sheath and predominates with immobilization of the repaired tendon. Collagen
deposition is disorganized.
Intrinsic tendon healing is accomplished via inflammatory cells and fibroblasts derived from
within the tendon and the epitenon. The intrinsic mechanism predominates if motion
rehabilitation is used postoperatively.
Biochemistry of tendon healing
Collagen synthesis
Collagen is synthesized by fibroblasts within tendon fascicles.
The predominant collagen type in tendon is type I.
The synthesis of collagen fibers includes intracellular and extracellular processes.
Posttranslational hydroxylation (in the ribosome) and glycosylation (in the Golgi body)
occur within the fibroblast.
Intermolecular cross-linking and triple helix formation also occur within the cell.
Fibril formation and intermolecular cross-linking occur within the extracellular matrix.
Binding of platelet-derived growth factor to receptors on the fibroblasts stimulates
fibroblast proliferation and differentiation and collagen production.
Vascular endothelial growth factor is detectable at the tendon repair site early in tendon
healing. Expression of vascular endothelial growth factor peaks at 7 to 10 days postinjury.
Subsequently, maximum vascular ingrowth occurs at 17 to 28 days postinjury.
Insulin-like growth factor 1 appears to increase cell proliferation at tendon repair sites
and increases collagen content in repaired tendon.
Integrins, cell surface molecules that mediate the interaction between fibroblasts and
their extracellular matrix, are upregulated for more than 2 weeks after tendon repair.

Etiology and Mechanism of Injury
Zone I injuries (FDP tendon alone) may result from a laceration or avulsion injury. The
mechanism of an avulsion usually is forced extension of a finger that is actively flexing
(eccentric contraction). Because this is commonly observed after attempted tackle when
grabbing a player’s jersey in American football, the injury commonly is referred to as a
jersey finger. Avulsion is most common in the ring finger.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:20 PM
AAOS | Hand and Wrist Flexor Tendon Repair and Reconstruction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004034
6/29

Zone II injuries are most likely to occur after a laceration. If the laceration occurred while
the digit was flexed, then the level of the volar skin laceration may not represent the true
level of the tendon injury. In this case, the tendon laceration may be distal to the level of
the skin laceration.
Zone III, zone IV, and zone V injuries often result from a laceration but also may result
from an attritional injury secondary to inflammatory conditions; fracture or nonunion; or
irritation by prominent metal implants, such as a plate and screws.
Rupture of the A2 pulley is an uncommon injury that can occur with an eccentric
contraction in a flexed position. This type of force is uncommon, except in sports such as
rock climbing.
Associated Injuries
Complex injuries may be associated with open fractures, soft-tissue deficits, and nerve and
arterial injuries.
Injury Classification
Flexor tendon injuries are classified into zones I through V.
Zone I is distal to the FDS insertion and is an injury of the FDP only.
Specific considerations for zone I injuries are as follows:
In a type I injury, the FDP is retracted into the palm. Both vincula are disrupted; therefore,
nutrition to the tendon is impaired. Repair more than 7 to 10 days postinjury is difficult
secondary to challenges retrieving the retracted tendon, passing it through the pulleys,
advancing the contracted muscle, and repairing the more friable tendon to its insertion
point.
In a type II injury, the FDP is observed at the level of the PIP joint, occasionally with a fleck of
bone attached. Repair within several weeks may yield satisfactory outcomes.
In a type III injury, the tendon is observed with a large bony fragment that prevents the
stump from retracting proximal to the A4 pulley. Similar to type II injuries, delayed repair
may be successful.

In a type IV injury, a volar avulsion fracture and a separate avulsion of the FDP tendon from
its insertion are present (Figure 3).
Type V injuries involve an FDP avulsion and an associated comminuted distal phalanx
fracture.
Figure 3 Lateral radiograph of a finger demonstrates a flexor digitorum profundus avulsion,
which in this case includes an intra-articular distal phalanx fracture. A fracture combined
with a flexor digitorum profundus avulsion that was retracted to the A2 pulley was not visible
on plain radiographs (making this a type IV injury). (Reproduced from Weiss LE, Fox MP,
Sweet S: Flexor tendon repair, in Colvin AC, Flatow E, eds: Atlas of Essential Orthopaedic
Procedures, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 428-
434.)
Specific considerations for zone II injuries are as follows:
Flexor tendon zone II injuries involve lacerations to the FDP and FDS tendons.
Because of historically poor outcomes, this zone was once termed no-man’s-land, and
primary repair was not recommended.
Improvements in surgical management, including suture techniques, appropriate and
judicious venting (excision or partial excision) of pulleys, and rehabilitation protocols, have

made good results possible in zone II; however, these are still troublesome injuries.
Optimal timing for repair of zone II injuries in a perfused digit is within 7 to 10 days
postinjury.
Urgent repair is indicated in patients with compromised perfusion.
Zone III is in the palm and denotes the origin of the lumbricals from the flexor tendon.
Zone IV is the region of the carpal tunnel.
Zone V lies over the distal forearm, distal to the musculotendinous junction (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Photograph of a hand shows the five zones of flexor tendon injury. Note the three
zones of the thumb. ( Copyright Fraser J. Leversedge MD, Durham, NC, Martin Boyer, MD, MSc,
FRCSC, St. Louis, MO, and Charles A. Goldfarb, MD, St. Louis, MO.)

Injury Classification
Zone I injuries may be an avulsion of the FDP tendon insertion from the volar base of the
distal phalanx or an avulsion fracture of the volar base of the phalanx. Such injuries,
termed jersey finger injuries, were originally classified by Leddy and Packer into three
subtypes (Figure 5). Currently, zone I injuries are classified into five subtypes.

Figure 5 Illustrations show the Leddy and Packer classification of profundus avulsions. In
type I injuries, the flexor digitorum profundus tendon is avulsed from its insertion and
retracts into the palm. In type II injuries, the profundus tendon is avulsed from its
insertion, but the stump remains within the digital sheath, implying that the vinculum
longum profundus is still intact. In type III injuries, a bony fragment is attached to the
tendon stump, which remains within the flexor sheath. Additional proximal retraction is
prevented at the distal end of the A4 pulley. (Reproduced with permission from Seiler JG
III: Flexor tendon injury, in Wolfe SW, Hotchkiss RN, Pederson WC, Kozin SH, Cohen MS,
eds: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, ed 7. Philadelphia, PA, Elsevier, 2017, vol 1, pp 183-
230.)
In zone II, the flexor sheath contains the tendons of the FDS and the FDP, and both
tendons may be completely or partially lacerated. This zone is most at risk for adhesions
after injury or tendon repair.
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Physical Examination
Initial evaluation of the injured hand should be performed before the administration of local
anesthesia or sedation.
Examination of the injured hand

Examination of the flexor tendons
Tenodesis is a good method to assess tendon integrity, especially in a patient who is sedated
or cannot cooperate with the physical examination. In the absence of flexor tendon
disruption, wrist extension should result in passive flexion of the digits at the MCP, PIP, and
DIP joints via tenodesis. Maintenance of a digit in an extended position at the PIP or DIP joint
with wrist extension indicates flexor tendon discontinuity.
Isolation of the FDP tendon of a digit is accomplished by maintaining the PIP joint in
extension and asking the patient to flex the digit; inability to flex the DIP joint of the digit
indicates an FDP injury.
Isolation of the FDS tendon is accomplished by maintaining the adjacent DIP joints in
extension and asking the patient to flex the finger toward the palm; inability to flex the PIP
joint of a digit with adjacent digits held in extension indicates an injury to the FDS tendon of
that digit.
Intact vincula may provide 60% to 90% of DIP and PIP joint motion in patients with a zone I
flexor tendon laceration. Tendon function is tested against resistance to elucidate intact
vincula.

Physical Examination
The physical examination should begin with observation of the resting position of the
hand and assessment of the digital cascade. Malalignment or malrotation of the digits
may be a sign of an underlying fracture. A neurovascular examination should be
performed given the proximity of the tendons, particularly the flexors, to the digital
neurovascular bundles. Assessment of skin integrity on the dorsal and palmar aspects of
the hand helps localize potential sites of tendon injury.
Lacerations near joints must be carefully inspected for evidence of traumatic
arthrotomy.
Neurovascular Examination
The radial and ulnar digital nerves are tested via two-point static discrimination.

Capillary refill of the volar digital pulp and the nail bed are assessed. Abnormal findings should
alert the surgeon to anticipate microvascular repair. Occasionally, Doppler devices or Doppler
ultrasonography may be used to assess for vascular patency of the digital vessels.

Neurovascular Examination
Ensure the patient understands the test. Practice on the uninjured digits or the other
hand to confirm understanding. Assessment of digital nerve continuity in young children
who cannot participate in two-point discrimination can be accomplished via immersion
of the hand in water and looking for wrinkling of the skin; however, in practice, this is
uncommonly used because the nerve of a child with a flexor tendon laceration will be
visually assessed intraoperatively.
Imaging Studies
Radiographs aid in assessing for concomitant fractures and avulsion injuries if the mechanism
of injury suggests this is a possibility.
In the acute setting, advanced imaging studies, such as ultrasonography and MRI, are not
usually helpful; however, they may aid in identifying associated pathology in patients with an
attritional rupture, establishing the extent of tendon retraction in a subacute laceration or
rupture, or evaluating for tenorrhaphy rupture. Pulley rupture may be assessed via MRI or
ultrasonography (Figure 6).
MRI or CT also is useful in patients with an attritional rupture to identify the primary cause (eg,
hook of hamate, scaphoid osteophyte).

Nonsurgical Management
Flexor tendon injuries associated with complex soft-tissue injury and fracture with extensive
comminution may not be suitable for primary repair. These injuries may benefit from delayed
or staged management.
Injuries associated with infection are not suitable for primary repair.
Closed pulley injuries that are acute and isolated to the A2 pulley may be managed
nonsurgically with the use of a pulley ring or via nonconstrictive circumferential digital taping
to prevent bowstringing of the flexor tendons as the pulley heals.
Surgical Management
Principles
Strickland described the ideal repair construct as having the following characteristics:
Easy suture placement
Secure knots
Smooth end-to-end apposition
Minimal to no gapping at the repair site
No injury to tendon vasculature
Adequate strength for early active postoperative motion1 (Resource 1)
Tendon handling should be minimized to reduce adhesion formation. A minimum of a four-
strand repair is recommended. The use of a supplemental epitendinous suture has been
suggested to coapt the tendons further and enhance tensile strength by 10% to 50%2
(Resource 2).
Partial or complete release (so-called venting) of the A4 pulley and/or partial release of the A2
pulley are methods to facilitate gliding of the repair construct, given that other pulleys are
structurally adequate3 (Resource 3)
Pulleys should not be preserved to sacrifice good tendon repair; rather, the surgeon may
judiciously partially release pulleys to facilitate exposure and repair of the tendons.
Techniques and Procedures
Preoperative Planning
In general, suspected or partial tendon lacerations in which flexor tendon function remains
fully intact rarely benefit from exploration and are most commonly observed; however, partial

9/3/26, 4:20 PM
AAOS | Hand and Wrist Flexor Tendon Repair and Reconstruction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004034
14/29

injuries that result in mechanical issues, such as triggering or tenosynovitis within the sheath
that limits tendon gliding, may warrant exploration. This is more commonly observed late
rather than acutely; however, either presentation is possible.
If a partial tendon laceration is encountered during exploration or surgical management for
some other indication, such as during nerve repair, controversy exists with regard to the
percentage of laceration that represents an indication for tendon repair. Some studies report
that as many as 90% of lacerations may be managed without repair, whereas more often
surgeons may consider repair of the tendon with the use of a core suture if more than 60% of
the tendon is disrupted.4-6
The rationale for not repairing a partial flexor tendon laceration includes the following
considerations:
Sutures add bulk.
The addition of sutures weakens the tendon, at least temporarily.
The gliding properties of the tendon are impaired with the addition of sutures.
The strength of flexor tendon repair at the time of repair is directly proportional to the number
of suture strands across the repair site.
Most commonly, a 3-0 or 4-0 core nonabsorbable suture is recommended.
Four-core-strand repair constructs have nearly twice the strength of two-strand repair
constructs.
Six-strand and eight-strand repairs add strength; however, they are technically challenging,
add manipulation of the tendon ends, add bulk, and may leave less tendon surface for end-
to-end healing.
A minimum of four strands in a core suture safely enables some active motion therapy
programs, such as place-and-active hold or full active half fist (Saint John Protocol).

Epitendinous sutures
In general, an epitendinous suture should be used if possible.
Epitendinous sutures improve tendon contour, enhance repair strength, and diminish gap
formation in flexor tendon repair constructs.
Most commonly, 6-0 monofilament suture is used.
An epitendinous simple running suture has lower tensile strength compared with
interlocking horizontal mattress or cross-stitch techniques.
Tension forces on tendons during digital flexion are greatest dorsally; therefore, dorsal-to-
midline placement of repair sutures is recommended.
The A2 and A4 pulleys are the most important for flexor tendon function. Results from a 2014
biomechanical study suggested that release of all of one pulley (A2 or A4) to facilitate tendon
gliding may not worsen clinical outcomes.3
Patient Positioning
The patient is placed in the supine position with the arm on a radiolucent hand table.
Regional or general anesthesia or local anesthesia with epinephrine (occasionally referred to
wide awake local anesthesia no tourniquet) can be used.
Assessment of tendon gliding and gap under stress is optimally performed with the patient
awake and actively moving the repaired tendon. If the suture is too loose, the repair may gap
with active motion as the suture bunches in the tendon and no longer serves to hold the
lacerated ends opposed (tendon gap). Problems uncovered via active motion in an awake
patient allow the surgeon the opportunity to revise the tenorrhaphy.
Surgical Approaches
Bruner and/or midlateral approaches may be used.
The location of the laceration may necessitate modifications to the standard incisions (Figure
8).

Special Considerations for Zone I Injuries
Repair techniques include reinsertion of the FDP tendon by using a suture anchor in the distal
phalanx or passing sutures that grasp the tendon dorsally through or around the distal
phalanx and tying them over the nail plate.
Larger bone avulsions usually are repaired via screw fixation.
Special Considerations for Zone II Injuries
Restoration of the orientation of the two slips of FDS in relation the FDP tendon (Camper
chiasm) is important; however, one slip of FDS can be excised to facilitate tendon gliding.
FDP-only may can decrease adhesion formation if a clean repair of both tendons is not
possible.
SEND FEEDBACK

Surgical Fracture Fixation
In zone I injuries, often the avulsion fracture, if present, is fixed via screw fixation (1.0 or 1.3
mm) in addition to the tendon repair technique.
Reliable fixation of fractures associated with tendon injuries may make exercises safer.
Postoperative Management
Postoperatively, a postoperative dorsal block splint is applied with the wrist and MCP joints
flexed and the PIP and DIP joints extended.
A supervised physical therapy program is initiated after a few days of rest.
Many variations in physical therapy programs exist, with ongoing debate about their relative
advantages and limitations. These may include passive flexion and active extension (with or
without dynamic splints), passive placement of the hand into a fist with active hold, or full
active motion to a half fist position.
A dorsal blocking splint is used for approximately 6 weeks postoperatively. The position of the
wrist can be flexed; however, a more neutral position has been advocated by some studies.3,7
The MCP joints are flexed.
Force is limited for 3 to 6 months postoperatively.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Avoid excessive handling of the tendon.
Do not remove the tendon from the sheath to retrieve it because the vincula may become
disrupted.
Partial or complete release of the A4 pulley and/or partial release of the A2 pulley can be
performed if the other pulleys are adequate if necessary to ensure tendon gliding.
Tendon Transfers
Preferred if the muscle powering a tendon is not functional or is substantially contracted or
patients in whom an attritional rupture has occurred over a segment of tendon (eg, using the
FDS tendon of the ring finger to reconstruct FPL insufficiency)
Transfers frequently are used to manage inflammatory and attritional ruptures.
Intercalary grafting may be used in certain scenarios as an alternative to transfer.
Tendon Reconstruction

Neglected tendon injuries and late referrals of acute injuries frequently are complicated by
contracture of the muscle-tendon unit and the presence of excessive scarring.
Under these circumstances and if acute tendon injury occurs with extensive or segmental
destruction of the tendon, the pulley system, or the tissue bed, secondary reconstruction
options are considered.
The reconstructive ladder for tendon reconstruction includes tendon transfer, single-stage
tendon reconstruction, and two-stage tendon reconstruction.
Single-stage tendon grafting
Indications
The FDS and FDP tendons are disrupted, repair is delayed, and proximal muscle and
tendon retraction has occurred without scarring.
Single-stage tendon grafting is not performed very often. It may be considered if a patient
has not undergone previous surgery or has substantial trauma to the flexor sheath.
In patients with an intact FDS tendon and a disrupted FDP tendon, surgeons must consider
the risk of compromising FDS function via adhesion formation.
Delayed reconstruction of an FDP tendon through a fully functioning FDS tendon is rarely
indicated, and a fully functioning FDS tendon should never be sacrificed to enable placement
of a primary graft.
In rare circumstances, FDP reconstruction with an intact FDS tendon may be considered in
younger patients and those with specific vocational or avocational requirements for DIP
flexion.
Two-stage flexor tendon reconstruction
Indications
Preferred in patients with severe crushing of adjacent soft-tissue structures, including the
pulley system, associated fractures requiring prolonged immobilization
Also preferred in patients in whom primary treatment was delayed or failed and in whom
extensive scarring is present.
Technique for tendon grafting
Stage 1
A silicone tendon implant is introduced proximally, threaded distally through the
remaining pulley system, and sutured to the FDP stump.
The proximal portion of the implant is guided into the forearm in a plane between the
FDS and FDP muscles.
After stage 1, early passive motion within a dorsal blocking splint allows for gliding of the
tendon implant to develop an organized sleeve of fibrous tissue, forming a pseudotendon

Stage 2 (after 3 months)
In the second procedure, the tendon graft is sutured to the proximal edge of the implant
and pulled distally through the newly developed sheath.
The implant is removed, and the distal insertion of the graft tendon is created.
The graft tendon is then repaired to the tendon of the FDP, which remains in the distal
forearm.
Donor Site Options for Tendon Grafting
Intrasynovial donor grafts
Tendon grafts from intrasynovial sources are associated with less tissue necrosis, less
expression of proinflammatory cytokines, and better preservation of gliding.
The FDL of the second toe has the longest segment of intrasynovial tendon.
The Paneva-Holevich technique, using a surgically created end-to-end FDS–FDP repair in the
palm, takes advantage of an intrasynovial tendon graft.
Extrasynovial tendon grafts
Associated with increased adhesions, greater early cellular necrosis, and a rise in repair site
inflammatory cytokines
Common extrasynovial graft tendons include the palmaris longus tendon and the plantaris
tendon, or the toe extensors.
Complications
Infection
May compromise the tendon repair and may result in the need for multiple débridements and
staged reconstruction
Surgeons must consider carefully if reconstruction is indicated after the infection resolves.
Various factors must be considered regarding reconstruction after infection, including
adequate soft-tissue envelope, functional digital arteries, fingertip sensibility, associated
osteomyelitis and/or pyarthrosis, fixed joint contracture, disproportionate symptoms and

Tendon Adhesions
Despite adequate tendon repair, therapy programs, and splinting programs, adhesion
formation is common after flexor tendon repair.
Factors associated with increased adhesion formation include repair constructs within the
synovial flexor sheath, extensive crush injuries, excessive surgical manipulation, associated
fractures and infections, and reconstruction of failed primary repair.
If a supervised physical therapy program, including home exercises, are performed well for
many months and limited active flexion and an intact repair construct are present, surgical
management to release adhesions (tenolysis) may be considered.
Tenolysis
Indications—The ideal candidate for tenolysis is a patient with localized tendon adhesions
and full passive digital motion who is motivated to perform exercises immediately
postoperatively.
Tenolysis in combination with other procedures that require postoperative immobilization
(eg, nerve repair, bone grafting) is discouraged.
In general, tenolysis is not performed earlier than 3 to 6 months after a tendon repair
because of the following:
Increased risk of tendon rupture if performed prematurely
Potential to overcome adhesions via effective and frequent physical therapy exercises
alone.
Tendon Rupture
Predisposing factors include inadequate repair and nonadherence to activity restrictions.
Mean reported re-rupture rate is approximately 5%.
Acute recognition and timely exploration may allow for revision repair under ideal
circumstances (eg, absence of infection, patient compliance, adequate soft-tissue conditions).
Tendon reconstruction is preferred for the management of late rupture and ruptures
associated with excessive scarring.
Rerupture occurs most frequently occur during the first 7 to 10 days postoperatively, and the
risk decreases after approximately 3 weeks.

Joint Contracture
Reported rates of contracture are as high as 17%.
May result from scarring of the volar plate, bowstringing because of pulley incompetence,
associated fractures, skin contractures, and tendon adhesion.
Early identification, stretching exercises, and splinting may help manage developing
contracture.
Stretching exercises (occasionally performed under a supervised physical therapy program
with home-based exercises) may be effective for more than 1 year.
Surgical management may be considered if the degree of contracture limits function.
The surgical technique involves checkrein ligament release, sequential palmar-to-dorsal
collateral ligament release, and volar plate release if necessary.
Late Complications
Swan neck deformity
Isolated loss of the FDS tendon rarely results in substantial functional loss.
If combined with loss of integrity of the PIP joint volar plate, hyperextension of the PIP joint
with flexion of the DIP joint results in a swan neck deformity.
With lateral band dorsal subluxation, the patient may have impairment with initiation of
flexion, which may yield a false picture of flexor tendon dysfunction.
Tenodesis of the remaining stump of the FDS tendon to the proximal phalanx prevents this
deformity.
Triggering
Triggering after flexor tendon repair (or after a partial flexor tendon laceration) may occur if
the bulk of the healed tendon is too large for the tendon sheath and catches or locks.
Occasionally, reduction tenoplasty, venting of a noncritical pulley, or partial FDS excision (for
injuries proximal to zone I) may be considered.
Lumbrical plus finger
Paradoxical extension of the interphalangeal joints of the injured digit with attempted flexion
is termed the lumbrical plus deformity.
Loss or lengthening of the portion of the FDP tendon distal to the lumbrical origin results in
force transmission through the lumbrical tendon (and to the distal phalanx) rather than the
flexor.
Via its insertion onto the radial band, the lumbrical tendon acts as an extensor of the
interphalangeal joints.

Management involves release or excision of the lumbrical tendon.
Quadriga
Quadriga is the inability of uninjured fingers of the same hand to attain full flexion.
May result from functional shortening of the FDP tendon because of retraction or
overtightening during repair.
Because the long, ring, and little fingers have a common muscle belly, the proximal excursion
of the FDP tendons to these digits extends only as far as the shortest tendon allows.
Loss of tendon excursion prevents full digital flexion in the adjacent digits, which manifests
as weakness of grip.
Postoperative Management
Principles
The evolution of physical therapy programs after tendon laceration followed the development
of stronger suture techniques, better understanding of tendon nutrition and healing, and
better understanding of the response of tendon to stress.
Motion of a repaired tendon unit results in the predominance of intrinsic healing over extrinsic
tendon healing and reduces adhesions.
Tendon Motion Protocols
Passive motion protocols
Low force and low excursion
Kleinert technique—Uses a dorsal block splint with the wrist in 45° of flexion and elastic
bands secured to the patient’s nails and a more proximal attachment point. After the
interphalangeal joints are actively fully extended, recoil of the elastic bands flexes them
down passively.
Duran protocol—Uses a splint with the wrist in 20° of flexion. Relies on the patient to
passively extend the DIP and PIP joints alternately, with the other joints of the finger flexed to
draw the repaired FDS and FDP tendons away from the repair site.
Early active motion protocols
Moderate force and potentially high excursion
Protocols involve generating light muscle forces to assist in digital flexion.
Place and active hold exercises often are the first stage.
Most use a dorsal blocking splint that limits wrist extension to slight flexion or neutral.

Theoretically, early re-rupture and gap formations are higher but are low with good surgical
repair technique and patient adherence to recommended activity restrictions.
Compared with passive exercise protocols, early active range of motion protocols result in an
increase in joint motion, equal rates of tendon rupture, and fewer substantial flexion
contractures.
Synergistic motion regimen
Low force and high tendon excursion
Passive digit flexion is combined with active wrist extension, followed by active digit
extension coupled with active wrist flexion.
Tendon excursion using wrist motion is greater than that provided in an extension blocking
splint.
Exercises from least to greatest tensile force: passive protected digit extension (2 to 4 N), place
and hold (3 to 9 N), active composite fist (9 to 20 N), hook and straight fist (8 to 13 N), isolated
joint motion (19 N), resistive composite fist, resistive hook and straight, and resistive isolated
joint (49 to 65+ N)
Rupture of repair most frequently occurs during the first 7 to 10 days postoperatively.
Immobilization protocols
Prolonged immobilization is reserved for children and patients unable to comply with the
motion protocols previously described.
Casts or splints are applied with the wrist and MCP joints positioned in flexion and the
interphalangeal joints in extension.
Initial casts are worn for 3 weeks postoperatively and later changed to splints, allowing for
serially increasing degrees of wrist and MCP joint extension.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Surgical treatment with the patient under local anesthesia may aid in assessment of bulkiness
and gliding and the gap of the repair.
Factors believed to reduce adhesions include limited handling of the tendons, confirmation of
an appropriate strong repair interface that facilitates early motion protocols, and hemostasis.
Stable skeletal fixation facilitates early exercises. Suboptimal reduction of fractures affecting
the fibro-osseous canal may contribute to adhesions.
Multistrand core suture, usually a running circumferential epitendinous suture, is preferred.
Dilation of pulleys may be useful, and partial release of the A4 pulley may be useful.

If a FDP stump of less than 1 cm is present, FDP advancement and repair to bone should be

Lacerations of slips of the FDS require different repair techniques than those used for the FDP.
Excision of a slip of FDS rather than repair of the FDS may be acceptable.
Future Directions
Recent interest has focused on diminishing tendon adhesions postoperatively via biologic
treatment options intraoperatively (with suggested use of hyaluronic acid, lubricin, 5-
fluorouracil) or orally (ibuprofen, celecoxib). These measures remain under investigation.
Regulation and/or application of growth factors to improve results remain under investigation.
Tissue engineering (biologic modification) of acellular allograft flexor tendons remains under
investigation.
